title: Pradakshina

segments.voice: Yesterday, darshan: to see and to be seen. Your line was see. Did you really look at one person, and let them look back? Day one hundred and thirty-four.

Remember the race around the world, back on day twenty-five? Ganesha and his brother Kartikeya are told that whoever circles the world first wins. Kartikeya jumps on his peacock and flies off across oceans and mountains. Ganesha, on his little mouse, simply walks around his parents, Shiva and Parvati, and says: you are my world. He wins. It's a story children love. And it's also a set of instructions, because Hindus walk around what they love all the time. Around shrines. Around trees. Around whole mountains. Today: pradakshina.
screen: `GANESHA CIRCLES HIS PARENTS.` → `YOU ARE MY WORLD.` → `TODAY: PRADAKSHINA.`

segments.voice: Pradakshina means walking around something holy, clockwise. The word holds the direction inside it: dakshina means the right hand, the right side. So you walk keeping the sacred on your right, the side of respect, with the center always in the center. After darshan at the front of the temple, many people turn and walk around the inner shrine. Many temples build a path for exactly this, a corridor that loops around the sanctum. Some people do one round, some three, some more, often a number that's meaningful to them or their family. And it doesn't stop at the temple walls. People circle the sacred tulsi plant in the courtyard, or a great fig tree. Some circle whole mountains. At Arunachala, in Tamil Nadu, pilgrims walk all the way around the holy hill, a journey of many miles, often barefoot, often at night under the full moon. Even a Hindu wedding has a circle at its heart: the couple walks around the sacred fire. Why walk in a circle? Think about what it does. A straight line goes somewhere else. A circle keeps coming back to the same center. Every step, the holy is right there beside you, and you can't lose sight of it. And there's Ganesha's point: the thing you circle becomes your world. Some people, at the end of their home puja, simply turn once in place, clockwise, when there's no room to walk. It's the same act, made small. The center stays the center.
screen: `DAKSHINA: THE RIGHT SIDE.` · `A PATH AROUND THE SANCTUM.` · `TREES, FIRE, WHOLE MOUNTAINS.` · `A CIRCLE KEEPS THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Stand up, if you can. Choose a center: a chair, a table, your corner, or just the spot where you were sitting. Now walk slowly around it, clockwise, keeping it on your right. Feel each step. Let the center stay in the corner of your eye the whole time. One round. If there's room, two more. If there's no room, turn once in place, clockwise. If walking is hard today, trace a slow circle with your hand. Then sit back down at the center. The bell holds the time.
Pradakshina. Walking clockwise around something holy, keeping it on your right, so the center stays the center. Today's word.
Your line: around. Today, notice what your day keeps circling, and whether it's what you'd choose to keep on your right. Day one hundred and thirty-four.

howItsDone: After darshan, many Hindus walk clockwise around the inner shrine of a temple, keeping the deity on their right, and some also circle sacred trees, the tulsi plant, or holy hills such as Arunachala; at home, some turn once in place at the end of puja.

original.note: Sanskrit pradakṣiṇā: moving around with the right side toward the center; circumambulation.

trapdoor: what you thought: walking around a temple.
what it means: circling the holy clockwise, keeping it on your right, so it stays at the center of your path, and your world.
what a scholar hears: pradakṣiṇa is from dakṣiṇa, right or southern; temples build a pradakshina patha around the garbhagriha, and giri pradakshina of Arunachala is a major pilgrimage practice.
